reference.source: ESC/ERS Guidelines for Pulmonary Hypertension / Nunn's Applied Respiratory Physiology
clinicalPearls: Constitutes group 4 pulmonary hypertension and is the pre-capillary form that is potentially curable by surgery, making its identification essential in every patient
Results from incomplete resolution of pulmonary emboli that organise into fibrotic material obstructing the pulmonary arteries, though many patients have no documented prior acute event
Presents with progressive exertional breathlessness and fatigue, sometimes with signs of right heart failure, developing months to years after a thromboembolic insult
The ventilation-perfusion scan is the key screening test, showing multiple segmental mismatched perfusion defects, and is more sensitive than CT pulmonary angiography for excluding the disease
Diagnosis requires persistent pulmonary hypertension despite at least several months of therapeutic anticoagulation, confirmed at right heart catheterisation
Lifelong anticoagulation is standard, and patients should be assessed at an experienced centre to determine operability

Pulmonary endarterectomy is the treatment of choice for surgically accessible disease and can be curative; balloon pulmonary angioplasty and targeted medical therapy help inoperable or residual disease
reference.pathophysiology: Chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension develops when acute pulmonary thromboembolism fails to resolve and instead organises into fibrous, endothelialised material that becomes incorporated into the pulmonary arterial wall, producing webs, bands, and stenoses that mechanically obstruct flow. Over time a secondary small-vessel arteriopathy develops in non-obstructed territories, resembling the remodelling of arterial pulmonary hypertension and contributing to the rise in pulmonary vascular resistance. The chronically obstructed and remodelled circulation imposes a progressive afterload on the right ventricle, leading to hypertrophy, dilatation, and eventual failure. Because the proximal obstructing material is fibrotic rather than fresh clot, it is amenable to surgical removal, which distinguishes the disorder from other forms of pulmonary hypertension.
additionalDifferentials: Idiopathic or heritable pulmonary arterial hypertension
Pulmonary hypertension due to left heart disease (group 2)
Pulmonary hypertension due to lung disease or hypoxia (group 3)
In situ pulmonary artery sarcoma or tumour embolism
additionalInvestigations: Ventilation-perfusion scintigraphy as the primary screen for mismatched perfusion defects
Right heart catheterisation to confirm pre-capillary haemodynamics and quantify severity
Pulmonary angiography (conventional or CT/MR) to define the anatomy and surgical accessibility of obstruction
Transthoracic echocardiography to assess right ventricular function and estimate pressures
Thrombophilia and antiphospholipid antibody screening given the thromboembolic basis
Cardiopulmonary exercise testing and six-minute walk distance for functional and prognostic assessment
redFlags: Syncope or presyncope on exertion suggesting critically limited pulmonary flow
Signs of decompensated right heart failure with hypotension or hepatic congestion
Haemoptysis, which may reflect enlarged bronchial collaterals
Persisting or worsening pulmonary hypertension despite adequate anticoagulation, mandating operability assessment
reference.prognosis: Untreated, chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension carries a poor prognosis that worsens with rising pulmonary vascular resistance, but pulmonary endarterectomy can normalise haemodynamics and offer a functional cure in operable disease. Inoperable or residual disease is managed with balloon pulmonary angioplasty and targeted therapy at expert centres, with outcomes that continue to improve.
pitfalls: Relying on CT pulmonary angiography alone, which can miss disease that a ventilation-perfusion scan would detect
Attributing symptoms to residual acute embolism and not screening breathless patients months after an event
Labelling disease inoperable without assessment at an experienced surgical centre
Starting targeted pulmonary vasodilator therapy in an operable patient and thereby delaying curative surgery
Failing to establish lifelong anticoagulation and investigate an underlying thrombophilia
references: ESC/ERS Guidelines for the Diagnosis and Treatment of Pulmonary Hypertension
management: Lifelong therapeutic anticoagulation as the baseline treatment for all patients
Pulmonary endarterectomy as the treatment of choice and potential cure for operable proximal fibrotic obstruction
Balloon pulmonary angioplasty for inoperable, distal or residual disease
Targeted medical therapy with the soluble guanylate cyclase stimulator riociguat for inoperable or persistent pulmonary hypertension
Mandatory assessment at an experienced centre to determine operability
Management of right heart failure with diuretics and supplemental oxygen for hypoxaemia
Thrombophilia and antiphospholipid antibody evaluation given the thromboembolic basis
Functional surveillance with right heart catheterisation, echocardiography and exercise testing, supported by pulmonary rehabilitation
